headlines: Senate Republicans' revised Clarity Act won Trump's backing on stricter ethics rules, including mandatory divestment or blind trusts and no sunset date, ahead of Tuesday's 60-vote cloture threshold that needs 7 Democratic crossovers.

Bernstein says markets have "definitely not priced in" potential passage surprise, while Galaxy raised odds from 10% to 25%—but traders still peg passage at just 26% due to remaining amendments, House reconciliation, and December 31 deadline.
Bitcoin climbed as AI slowdown calls from industry leaders tanked Nvidia and Intel stock, while Trump dismissed tighter AI controls and defended data centers as unnecessary.
Strategy halted Bitcoin buybacks for a second week despite slowing its preferred-stock repurchase from $176 million to $139 million, keeping crypto holdings frozen.

sections.title: The Clarity Act's Final Push
points: Senate Republicans released a revised "last, best and final" offer on Sunday that includes 126 Democratic demands: divestment or blind trusts for crypto executives, state attorney general enforcement authority, and no sunset date—concessions Trump previously resisted.

The bill dropped criminal-prosecution protections for decentralized finance (DeFi—a financial system running on blockchain without traditional intermediaries) but added "circuit breaker" language allowing Treasury to restrict stablecoin (cryptocurrency pegged to stable assets like the U.S. dollar) rewards if deposits flee community banks.

Tuesday's cloture vote (a procedural vote to end debate and move to a floor vote) needs 60 votes; Republicans control 53 seats, requiring at least 7 Democratic votes to advance. Even if it passes, amendments, final passage, and House reconciliation must all complete by December 31.

sections.title: Market Skepticism Despite Momentum
points: Bernstein told clients that "any positive surprise is definitely not priced in," suggesting crypto assets could rally significantly if the bill passes.
Galaxy's Alex Thorn raised 2026 passage probability from 10% to 25%, but traders on prediction markets still assign only 26% odds, reflecting doubts about clearing multiple legislative hurdles.
TD Cowen analyst Jaret Seiberg notes Democrats are receiving a finished product rather than negotiating directly, which could reduce their incentive to cross party lines.
